title: Horrible headache: recurrent one-sided headache with visual disturbance in a 24-year-old university student on the combined pill
desc: This station involves a focused history and a focused neurological examination of a 24-year-old university student in general practice. She has a severe, throbbing left-sided headache today, her fifth similar attack, each one preceded by visual disturbance. The candidate then interprets her observations and a urine pregnancy test, diagnoses migraine with aura, and explains a general practice management plan to her. The plan covers treatment of attacks, stopping the combined oral contraceptive pill because of the stroke risk, trigger management, prevention, study support and safety netting.
focus: Taking a headache history that separates a primary from a dangerous secondary headache, diagnosing migraine with aura, and recognising that it rules out the combined oral contraceptive pill
diagnosis: Combined oral contraceptive pill contraindicated (migraine with aura)
stem: You are a final-year medical student on placement in a general practice. Helen Brooks, a 24-year-old university student, has come in with a headache. The practice nurse has noted that Helen does not smoke, drink alcohol or use recreational drugs, has no known family history of illness, exercises regularly and eats a healthy diet. You do not need to ask about these again. Your GP supervisor will see her after you.
tasks: Take a focused history from Helen and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Helen's observations and urine pregnancy test. Hand over to your supervisor with your interpretation, give your diagnosis and differentials, then explain your management plan to Helen and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Helen Brooks, a 24-year-old university student. You have had a bad headache since this morning and are in obvious pain. The room light bothers you: you squint, and you speak quietly. You are frustrated and worried about your studies. If the candidate offers to dim the lights or speak more softly, thank them. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: “I have this horrible headache!”

The headache (give only when asked):

  • Site: the left side of your forehead.
  • Radiation: it spreads towards your left temple. It does not go to the right side.
  • Onset: it started this morning, 4 to 5 hours ago, and built up gradually. It was not sudden. It did not come on like being hit on the head.
  • Character: throbbing.
  • Severity: 8 to 9 out of 10. It is not the worst headache of your life: “it’s just like the other ones.”
  • Previous episodes: you have had 4 similar headaches before, all since this semester started about 3 months ago. Each lasted 6 to 7 hours and then went away completely. You feel normal between them.
  • Worse with: loud noise and bright light.
  • Better with: lying down in a dark, cool room.

Before the headache (give only if asked about warning signs or anything before the pain, or about vision): about half an hour before the pain started this morning, the lines on your lecture notes went “all jumbled” and you saw bright dots in your vision. They spread slowly and lasted about 20 minutes, then went completely before the headache started. The same thing happened before each of the earlier headaches.

Other symptoms (give each only when the candidate names it):

  • Light hurts your eyes: yes.
  • Noise bothers you: yes.
  • Nausea: yes, but you have not vomited.
  • Trouble concentrating: yes, during and after the headaches.
  • Tiredness: yes, you feel washed out for the rest of the day.

Say no if asked about: numbness, pins and needles or tingling; weakness in your face, arm or leg; slurred speech or trouble finding words; double vision or a drooping eyelid; loss of vision that does not come back; fever, a stiff neck or a rash; any head injury; a tight band around your head; a red, watering eye or a runny or blocked nose with the headache; pacing around with the pain; pain in your jaw when chewing or a tender scalp; headache that is worse in the morning or on coughing or straining; confusion or blackouts.

If asked about stress: you are very stressed about university, but the headache does not feel like a tight band.

Past medical history: none.

Medicines: the combined oral contraceptive pill, every day, for about 3 years. You take it for contraception. You are sexually active with your boyfriend (say this if asked why you take it). If asked, you take it every day and have not missed any pills. For the earlier headaches you took paracetamol once or twice, and it helped “a little”. You have taken nothing today. No other medicines or supplements.

Allergies: none.

Family history: nothing that you know of. Nobody in your family has migraines.

Social history (if asked):

  • You run 3 times a week and eat a balanced diet. Your height is 165 cm and your weight 55 kg (BMI 20).
  • You are very busy and stressed about classes and exams.
  • Only if asked about sleep, meals or caffeine: you have been sleeping less during assessment weeks and sometimes skip breakfast. You drink two coffees a day.
  • No smoking, alcohol or recreational drugs (the nurse already has this).

Ideas, concerns and expectations:

  • Idea (if asked what you think is causing it): “I’m not sure.”
  • Impact (if asked how it affects you): you often miss university classes because of the headaches.
  • Concern: “I’m really worried I’m going to fail my course.”
  • Expectation: you want to know what is going on and how to stop the headaches.

Question to raise near the end of Part 1: “Can you give me something for it now?” Accept an answer that something will be given or planned.

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they are examining):

  • General inspection: a well-looking young woman in obvious pain. She squints in the light and holds her head still. Not pale or flushed. No rash.
  • Observations (practice nurse, on arrival): HR 77/min, regular. BP 135/85 mmHg. Temperature 37.0 °C. RR 15/min. SpO2 99% on room air. (The nurse's full set, with a repeat, is handed over in Part 2.)
  • Meningism: no neck stiffness. Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s signs negative. No rash on the skin.
  • Fundoscopy: she finds the light uncomfortable but cooperates. Both optic discs pink with sharp margins, and spontaneous venous pulsations present. No haemorrhages.
  • Eyes (CN II, III, IV, VI): visual acuity 6/6 in each eye. Visual fields full to confrontation in each eye. Pupils equal and reactive to light, with no ptosis. Eye movements full, with no double vision and no nystagmus.
  • Other cranial nerves: facial sensation and movement normal and symmetrical. Speech normal. Palate and tongue normal.
  • Limbs: no pronator drift. Tone, power (5/5), reflexes and sensation normal and symmetrical in all four limbs. Plantar responses flexor.
  • Coordination and gait: finger-nose and heel-shin normal. Gait normal, including heel-to-toe walking. Romberg negative.
  • Head and neck: temporal arteries pulsatile and non-tender. Sinuses non-tender. No tenderness of the scalp, neck muscles or jaw joints.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Helen's identity, and explains the examination and gains consent.
Is empathic to her pain and distress: offers to dim the lights or speak quietly, acknowledges her worry about failing her course, and uses plain language.
History
Characterises the headache:

kids.x: Site and radiation: left frontal, spreading to the left temple, not to the right.
Onset: started this morning, 4 to 5 hours ago, and built up gradually; asks specifically whether it was sudden (thunderclap) [it was not].
kids.d: Award only if the speed of onset is asked about.

kids.x: Character and severity: throbbing, 8 to 9 out of 10, not the worst ever.
Aggravating and relieving factors: worse with loud noise and bright light; better lying in a dark, cool room.
Pattern: 4 previous similar headaches in about 3 months, each lasting 6 to 7 hours, and well between them.

check.x: Asks about a warning before the headache and characterises the aura: jumbled lines and bright dots that spread over about 20 minutes, resolved completely before the headache, and occurred before each attack.
Asks about associated features: sensitivity to light and noise, nausea without vomiting, difficulty concentrating, fatigue.
check.d: Award if at least three are asked about.

check.x: Screens for focal neurological symptoms: numbness or tingling, weakness, speech change, double vision or a drooping eyelid, persistent visual loss [all absent].
Asks questions to exclude other causes of headache:
check.d: Each kid is marked separately; kid 1 (meningitis screen) is critical.

kids.x: Tension-type headache: stress, a band-like tightness [very stressed, but not band-like].
Cluster headache: red, watering eye, runny nose, restlessness [none].
Raised intracranial pressure or giant cell arteritis: worse in the morning or on straining, vomiting, jaw pain on chewing, scalp tenderness [none].

check.x: Takes a medication history: identifies the combined oral contraceptive pill taken daily for contraception (sexually active), and asks about analgesic use [paracetamol once or twice; nothing today].
Asks about past medical history and allergies [both nil]. (Family history is given in the stem; credit, but do not require, a check for migraine in the family.)
Asks about migraine triggers: stress, sleep, skipped meals and caffeine [stressed about exams, sleeping less in assessment weeks, sometimes skips breakfast, two coffees a day].
check.d: Award for asking about at least two of stress, sleep, skipped meals or caffeine. Diet quality and exercise are in the stem and are not required.

check.x: Explores ideas, concerns, expectations and impact: unsure of the cause, often misses classes, worried she will fail her course, wants the headaches to stop.
Examination
Does a general inspection and reviews the observations, including temperature and blood pressure [in pain and photophobic; afebrile; BP 135/85].
Examines for meningism: neck stiffness, Kernig's or Brudzinski's sign, and a check of the skin for a rash [none].
Performs or offers fundoscopy, looking for papilloedema [discs sharp, venous pulsations present].
Examines the eyes: visual acuity, visual fields in each eye, pupils, ptosis and eye movements [all normal].
Examines the other cranial nerves, including facial movement and speech [normal].
Examines the limbs: pronator drift, tone, power, reflexes, sensation and plantar responses [normal, no hemiparesis].
Assesses coordination and gait, including heel-to-toe walking [normal].
Palpates the temporal arteries, sinuses, neck and jaw joints [non-tender].
Interpretation

Interprets the observations as normal: afebrile, normal heart rate, and a blood pressure that settles from 135/85 to 124/78 on the repeat, so she is not hypertensive. No sign of infection or of a hypertensive cause.
Interprets the urine pregnancy test as negative, so she is not pregnant and medicines and a change of contraception can be started today.

Gives migraine with aura as the most likely diagnosis, justified by recurrent attacks lasting hours, one-sided throbbing severe pain, light and noise sensitivity, nausea, and fully reversible visual aura before the headache, with a normal examination.
Names differentials, each with a feature for or against from this case: tension-type headache, cluster headache, subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis and TIA.
check.d: Award for at least three, including at least one dangerous secondary cause, each justified.

check.x: States that no brain imaging or blood tests are needed because there are no red flags (gradual onset, a stereotyped recurrent pattern, afebrile, normal neurological examination and fundi).
Management
Explains migraine in plain language (common, recurrent, not dangerous or a tumour) and offers written information (Healthdirect).
Plans treatment of attacks, including today's:

kids.x: Treats the attack early: aspirin 900 to 1000 mg soluble, ibuprofen 400 mg or paracetamol 1 g, with metoclopramide 10 mg orally, and rest in a dark, quiet room.
Adds a triptan (e.g. sumatriptan 50 to 100 mg orally) for severe attacks or if simple analgesia fails, taken when the headache starts, not during the aura.

check.x: Addresses contraception:

kids.x: Advises stopping the combined pill because migraine with aura plus oestrogen increases the risk of ischaemic stroke.
Offers a progestogen-only method (implant, hormonal IUD, injection or progestogen-only pill) or a copper IUD, switching without a gap, with condoms in the meantime as needed.
kids.d: Award only if an alternative is offered so she is not left without contraception.

check.x: Advises a headache diary and trigger management (sleep, meals, caffeine, stress, keep exercising), warns about medication-overuse headache (limit the days pain relief is taken), and a preventive (propranolol, amitriptyline or pizotifen) if attacks stay frequent or disabling.
check.d: Score from question 3 or 4, wherever it is said.

check.x: Supports her studies: offers a medical certificate for missed classes or special consideration, and suggests university student support or disability services.
Safety netting

Names red flags in plain words that need ED or 000: a sudden, severe 'worst ever' headache; fever with a stiff neck or rash; persistent vomiting; weakness, numbness or trouble speaking; visual loss or aura lasting over an hour or not going away; confusion or drowsiness.
check.d: Award for at least four, with ED or 000.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: GP review in about 2 to 4 weeks with the headache diary, the contraception change in place (for example an implant appointment) and a review of the response to treatment, and to come back sooner if attacks become more frequent or different, or treatment is not working.
check.d: Award for a GP review in about 2 to 4 weeks plus at least two of: bring the diary, confirm the new contraception is in place, review response to treatment, return sooner if attacks change or treatment fails.

part2.lead: Here are Helen's observations from the practice nurse, including a repeat set at the end of your consultation, and the urine pregnancy test the nurse did before any change to her medicines.
part2.patient:
• When the candidate explains the plan, ask: “Why do I have to stop the pill? I really don’t want to get pregnant.” Settle if the candidate explains the stroke risk simply and offers another method.
  • Then ask: “Do I need a brain scan?”
  • At the fourth question, after the examiner has put it, ask: “I’ve already missed so many classes. What do I do about my exams?”

handover.label: Observations (practice nurse, today)
handover.result: On arrival, and a repeat set at the end of the consultation. Seated, room air. Helen still has her headache.
handover.model:
• Read: RR 15 then 14, SpO2 99% on room air, HR 77 then 72 and regular, temperature 37.0 then 36.9 °C, alert. BP 135/85 on arrival, 124/78 on the repeat. Pain 8 out of 10 on both sets. All values are within normal adult ranges, so no escalation is needed.
  • For Helen: she is afebrile, which argues against meningitis or another infection. The first BP was taken while she was in severe pain and settled on the repeat, so she is not hypertensive; the combined pill is stopped because of her aura, not her blood pressure. A hypertensive cause of headache is unlikely.
  • What it changes: she is stable and can be managed in general practice. Recheck her BP at follow-up.

rows.note: Repeat set, seated, end of consultation

handover.label: Urine pregnancy test (point of care, today)
handover.result: Point-of-care urine test, performed by the practice nurse at 10:10 on a random urine sample. Control line present (valid test).
handover.model:
• Read: urine beta-hCG negative, with a valid control.
  • For Helen: she is not pregnant, so pregnancy is not a factor in her headaches, and aspirin or an NSAID, metoclopramide and a triptan can all be used; these choices would be restricted if she were pregnant.
  • What it changes: acute treatment (aspirin or ibuprofen, metoclopramide, a triptan) can be prescribed, and she can switch from the combined pill straight to a progestogen-only method or a copper IUD today. If there has been any unprotected sex since a missed pill, a repeat test in about 3 weeks would be needed. That is not the case here: she takes the pill every day and has not missed any.

ask: You are now handing over to your GP supervisor. Please give an ISBAR handover of Helen Brooks, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Helen now, here in general practice, explaining your plan to her as you go.
Before Helen goes home, what would you tell her and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: medical student; Helen Brooks, 24, university student.
  • Situation: a severe (8 to 9/10) throbbing left frontal headache since this morning, gradual onset, preceded by 20 minutes of visual aura; her fifth similar attack in 3 months.
  • Background: light and noise sensitivity, nausea; no focal symptoms, fever or head injury. Otherwise well. On the combined pill. Stressed about exams and missing classes.
  • Assessment: normal neurological examination, fundi and meningism check. Observations normal, afebrile, BP settled to 124/78. Urine hCG negative. Likely migraine with aura; no red flags.
  • Recommendation: acute treatment now; stop the combined pill and switch without a gap to a progestogen-only method or copper IUD; headache diary; review in 2 to 4 weeks.

Most likely: migraine with aura. For: five stereotyped attacks lasting 6 to 7 hours; one-sided, throbbing and severe; worse with light and noise; nausea; reversible visual aura (jumbled lines, dots) for about 20 minutes before each headache; normal examination.

  • Tension-type headache: for: exam stress. Against: not band-like, one-sided, throbbing, with nausea and photophobia.
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage: for: severe. Against: gradual onset, same as previous attacks, normal examination.
  • TIA: for: visual symptoms on oestrogen. Against: positive, spreading, fully reversible visual phenomena; no weakness or numbness.
  • Cluster: against: 6 to 7 h, lies still, no autonomic features.
  • Meningitis: against: afebrile, no meningism.

1. Explain the diagnosis: migraine is common and recurrent, not dangerous or a tumour. Offer a leaflet (Healthdirect).
  2. Brain scan (if asked): not needed: gradual onset, same as previous attacks, afebrile, normal neurological examination and fundi, so no red flags.
  3. Today and future attacks: aspirin 900 to 1000 mg soluble, ibuprofen 400 mg or paracetamol 1 g early, with metoclopramide 10 mg orally; rest in a dark, quiet room. Add a triptan (sumatriptan 50 to 100 mg orally) for severe attacks or if simple analgesia fails; take when the headache starts, not during the aura.
  4. Contraception: stop the combined pill (oestrogen plus aura raises stroke risk); switch without a gap to an implant, a hormonal IUD, an injection, the progestogen-only pill or a copper IUD.

• Call 000 or go to ED: a sudden severe “worst ever” headache; fever with a stiff neck or rash; weakness, numbness or trouble speaking; confusion or drowsiness; an aura lasting more than an hour or vision not coming back.
  • Prevention: diary, regular sleep and meals, limit pain-relief days (medication overuse), a preventive if attacks stay frequent.
  • Studies: a medical certificate, special consideration, university student support.
  • Follow-up: GP review in 2 to 4 weeks with the diary; new contraception in place (for example an implant appointment); review the response to treatment. Come back sooner if attacks are more frequent or different, treatment is not working, she needs pain relief on more than a few days a week, or she has side effects.

ddx.for: Five stereotyped attacks of severe, one-sided throbbing headache lasting 6 to 7 hours, with light and noise sensitivity and nausea, each preceded by about 20 minutes of fully reversible visual aura, with a normal examination.
She is very stressed about university and exams.
ddx.against: The pain is one-sided, throbbing and severe, not band-like, and comes with nausea, photophobia, phonophobia and aura.
She is a young woman with attacks lasting 6 to 7 hours, she lies still rather than pacing, and she has no red, watering eye or blocked nose.

ddx.for: A severe headache of 8 to 9 out of 10.
ddx.against: The onset was gradual, it is the same as four previous attacks, and the neurological examination and fundi are normal.
She is afebrile, with no neck stiffness, negative Kernig's sign and no rash.

ddx.for: Transient visual symptoms in a woman taking oestrogen.
ddx.against: The visual symptoms are positive (dots, jumbled lines), spread gradually, resolve fully and are followed by headache, with no weakness, numbness or speech change and a normal examination.

guide:
In Part 1, give examination findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. A sensible split is about 6 minutes of history and 4 of examination. Helen describes the aura only if asked about a warning, anything before the pain, or her vision. She gives each associated symptom only when the candidate names it. Her smoking, alcohol, drug use, family history, diet and exercise are in the stem, so do not penalise a candidate who does not ask about them again. Item 11 is earned by asking about past medical history and allergies; family history is in the stem and is not required. Item 12 is earned by asking about triggers (stress, sleep, meals, caffeine). Each kid of item 9 is marked separately.

In Part 2, hand over both results together and ask the four questions in order. Score items 30 to 32 from question 3 (explaining the diagnosis with written information, acute treatment, and the contraception switch). Helen asks why she must stop the pill and whether she needs a scan while the candidate explains. Item 32 and item 28 can be earned from those replies. Score the prevention item (item 33, including medication overuse) from question 3 or 4. Score item 34 (studies) and the safety-netting items 36 and 37 from question 4.

A high-performing candidate establishes the gradual onset and stereotyped pattern, elicits and characterises the aura, screens for focal and meningitic features, finds the combined pill, and checks the fundi and for meningism. In Part 2 they diagnose migraine with aura, explain why no scan is needed, treat the attack, stop the combined pill without leaving her unprotected, and address her studies.

A borderline candidate never asks about aura or the speed of onset, misses the combined pill or does not see why it matters, orders a CT brain, or stops the pill without offering another method.
explain:
Primary or secondary headache?

The first job in any headache history is to look for features of a dangerous secondary cause. A useful screen is SNOOP:

  • S: systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss) or systemic disease.
  • N: neurological symptoms or signs.
  • O: sudden (thunderclap) onset.
  • O: older age at onset (over 50).
  • P: a change in pattern; positional headache; precipitated by coughing or straining; papilloedema; progressive headache; pregnancy.

Helen has none of these. Her headache built up gradually and matches four previous attacks. She is afebrile with no meningism, and her neurological examination and fundi are normal. Neuroimaging and blood tests are therefore not indicated.

Why this is migraine with aura

Migraine with aura needs at least two attacks with fully reversible visual, sensory, speech, motor, brainstem or retinal aura and at least three of these six: (1) at least one aura symptom spreads gradually over 5 minutes or more; (2) two or more aura symptoms occur in succession; (3) each aura symptom lasts 5 to 60 minutes; (4) at least one aura symptom is unilateral; (5) at least one aura symptom is positive; (6) the aura is accompanied, or followed within 60 minutes, by headache. Helen meets (1), (3), (5) and (6).

Helen's jumbled lines and bright dots spread over about 20 minutes, resolve completely, and come before every headache. Visual aura is the commonest type.

Her headache phase also has the features of migraine (ICHD-3 1.1 criteria): attacks lasting 4 to 72 hours with at least two of:

  • one-sided pain;
  • pulsating pain;
  • moderate or severe intensity;
  • worse with routine activity.

They also need nausea or vomiting, or both photophobia and phonophobia.

Aura with motor weakness (hemiplegic migraine), brainstem symptoms such as vertigo, slurred speech or double vision (migraine with brainstem aura), aura lasting over an hour, or a first aura without headache needs further assessment, including for TIA.

Differentials

  • Tension-type headache: a bilateral, band-like, pressing headache without nausea or marked photophobia. Stress is a shared trigger, but her features do not fit.
  • Cluster headache: short (15 to 180 minute) attacks of severe orbital pain with tearing, a red eye, a blocked nose and restlessness. It is more common in men.
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage: a sudden headache that reaches its peak within a minute. Gradual onset and a stereotyped history argue strongly against it.
  • Meningitis: fever, neck stiffness and rash. All are absent.
  • TIA: gives sudden, negative symptoms (loss of vision or power) rather than positive, spreading phenomena.
  • Giant cell arteritis: essentially only occurs over 50, so it is very unlikely at 24; the jaw and scalp questions mainly complete the screen of the head and neck.
  • Non-specific headache: a label to reserve when the features do not fit a defined type.

The results

The observations are normal and she is afebrile. Her blood pressure was raised slightly while she was in pain and settled on the repeat. The urine pregnancy test is negative, so medicines and a change of contraception can go ahead today.

Management: the general practice plan

A useful structure is the mnemonic DKA EMPIRE FS:

  • D: Diagnosis.
  • K: Knowledge (what she knows).
  • A: Attitudes (how she feels).
  • E: Educate (what the condition is, how common it is, why it happens, triggers and complications, with diagrams and leaflets).
  • M: Management (immediate, short and long term; lifestyle and medicines).
  • P: Prevention.
  • I: Information (Healthdirect, Better Health Channel).
  • R: Reinforce (teach-back).
  • E: Evaluate (other concerns).
  • F: Follow up.
  • S: Safety net.

Treating attacks (eTG):

  • Take simple analgesia early in the headache: aspirin 900 to 1000 mg (soluble) or an NSAID such as ibuprofen 400 mg, or paracetamol 1 g.
  • Add metoclopramide 10 mg orally for nausea; it also improves absorption. Metoclopramide can cause acute dystonic reactions, especially in young women; use it only for acute attacks and do not exceed 30 mg a day.
  • If this does not work, or first-line for severe, disabling attacks that simple analgesia has not controlled (as for Helen, whose attacks are 8 to 9 out of 10 and helped only a little by paracetamol), use a triptan such as sumatriptan 50 to 100 mg orally, with metoclopramide. In migraine with aura it is taken when the headache begins, not during the aura.
  • Rest in a dark, quiet room.
  • Avoid medication-overuse headache: simple analgesics should not be used on 15 or more days a month, or triptans on 10 or more days a month.

Contraception: migraine with aura is an absolute contraindication to combined hormonal contraception at any age. Under the UK Medical Eligibility Criteria (UKMEC, widely used as the reference in Australia) it is category 4, because oestrogen adds to the higher risk of ischaemic stroke that comes with migraine with aura. Helen should stop the combined pill and switch, without a gap, to a progestogen-only or non-hormonal method:

  • etonogestrel implant;
  • levonorgestrel IUD;
  • depot medroxyprogesterone;
  • progestogen-only pill;
  • copper IUD.

Long-acting reversible methods are the most effective. Condoms also protect against STIs. At 24 she is in the age group for opportunistic chlamydia testing, which can be offered at the follow-up visit.

Prevention:

  • Keep a headache diary to find triggers: stress, poor sleep, skipped meals, caffeine, alcohol.
  • Keep regular sleep and meals, and continue regular exercise.
  • Consider a preventive medicine if attacks stay frequent or disabling despite good acute treatment. eTG options include propranolol, amitriptyline, pizotifen and candesartan; topiramate reduces the effectiveness of hormonal contraception, and valproate should be avoided in women who could become pregnant. Oestrogen-containing treatments should be avoided.

Study support: a medical certificate, special consideration and university support services address her main concern and reduce stress, which is itself a trigger.

Safety netting

  • Call 000 or go to ED: a sudden severe headache; fever with neck stiffness or rash; persistent vomiting; weakness, numbness or speech change; aura lasting over an hour, or visual loss that does not recover; confusion; headache after a head injury.
  • Follow-up: GP review in 2 to 4 weeks with the diary, to check her response to treatment and confirm the new contraception is in place.
points: Ask how fast the headache started and whether it matches previous attacks. A gradual, stereotyped headache with a normal examination and no red flags (SNOOP) needs no imaging.
Always ask about aura. Migraine aura is positive (dots, zigzags, jumbled lines), spreads over 5 minutes or more, lasts 5 to 60 minutes, resolves fully and is usually followed by headache.

Migraine with aura is an absolute contraindication to the combined oral contraceptive pill (UKMEC category 4) because of the risk of ischaemic stroke. Switch to a progestogen-only or non-hormonal method without leaving a gap in protection.

Treat attacks early with aspirin, an NSAID or paracetamol plus metoclopramide. Use a triptan if this does not work, or first-line for severe, disabling attacks, taken at the onset of the headache, not during the aura.

Limit acute medicines to avoid medication-overuse headache. Use a headache diary to identify triggers, and consider a preventive (propranolol, amitriptyline, pizotifen) when attacks are frequent or disabling.

Explain the plan in steps (diagnosis, knowledge, attitudes, education, management, prevention, information, reinforce, evaluate, follow-up, safety net), and address the impact on the patient's life, such as a certificate and study support.
